AI voice scam traps mom in 5-hour kidnapping nightmare https://t.co/zGGLDvwT7f

I want you to think about the voice of someone you love. You know how that person sounds when they're laughing, and you also know the voice you would hear if they were terrified. So what would you do if your phone rang, and you heard that voice begging you for help? That's what happened to Deborah Del Mastro.

I recently sat down with Deborah on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast to hear her tell this story in her own words. Even after everything she has been through, you can hear how deeply the experience still affects her. Months after the scam, she also told a U.S. Senate committee that she remained "completely traumatized."

The California mother and Navy veteran was having breakfast with her husband when a local number appeared on her phone. The man on the other end claimed a Mexican drug cartel had taken her 37-year-old daughter Sarah. Then Deborah heard the voice that made the threat feel terrifyingly real. "It's my daughter's voice," she told me. "And she's having a panic attack."

For the next five and a half hours, the caller threatened Deborah and her family, sent her and her husband from place to place and demanded thousands of dollars. What Deborah didn't know was that the story unfolding on the phone was very different from what was actually happening to Sarah.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist.

See the classes and register at https://t.co/x1SwswUebZ

THE FAMILY GROUP CHAT IS A GOLDMINE FOR SCAMMERS

The phone call that changed everything

The call started strangely enough. "I get a local phone call, my area code," Deborah told me. When she answered, the man asked, "Who is this?" Deborah turned the question back on him, and he replied that he was "someone you need to talk to."

Then he asked whether Deborah's daughter was prone to panic attacks. That question immediately got her attention. Deborah could hear commotion in the background before the caller put someone else on the line. She heard Sarah. The voice was crying and struggling to breathe. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I'm so scared," Deborah remembers hearing. "It was exactly her voice," she told me.

There was another reason Deborah believed she was hearing her daughter. Sarah had recently gone through a breakup, and Deborah had heard her daughter sobbing like that only days earlier. The sound on the phone matched something painfully familiar, which made the call even more convincing.

Then came the threat of a Mexican drug cartel

The man told Deborah that Sarah had witnessed something she was never supposed to see in a parking lot. He claimed ties to a Mexican drug cartel and said Sarah had her phone out when she saw what happened. According to Deborah, his boss had ordered him to take her.

Then he told Deborah what they wanted. "They were going to sell her for $20,000 unless I could come up with the money," Deborah told me. The threat became even darker. She said the caller repeatedly talked about selling Sarah and suggested she could "pay her way in other ways," leaving Deborah terrified that the criminals could sexually traffic her daughter. At that point, she believed violent criminals had Sarah.

The scammer made sure Deborah stayed on the phone

One of his first instructions was to bring a phone charger. "He tells me that I better charge my phone or bring a phone charger because if my phone dies before we're finished, I'll never see her again," Deborah recalled. That told me a lot about how carefully this scam was run. The caller needed control. He demanded that Deborah keep the phone connected so he could hear what was happening around her. He wanted to know when she moved, what she was doing and who she was talking to.

At one point, Deborah muted the call so she could speak privately with her husband. The caller noticed and began screaming. He warned her against trying "funny business." Deborah told me, "He wants to keep my phone open right here so he can hear everything." That control continued for five and a half hours.

YOUR FAMILY COULD BE ONE PHONE CALL FROM A BANK SCAM

'Bargaining with the devil'

The caller initially wanted $20,000. Deborah didn't have it. "We just don't have that," she remembers telling him. So she started negotiating for what she believed was her daughter's life. "Now I'm bargaining with the devil," she told me. Deborah said she had roughly $2,000 in savings. The caller instructed her to go to a nearby Walmart and use MoneyGram to wire money to Mexico. She went, keeping the phone where he could hear everything happening around her.

The man warned that people were watching her in the parking lot and claimed undercover police officers were nearby. He also gave Deborah a story to use if anyone questioned the transfer. The caller told her to say she was helping a relative with medical expenses. "Be discreet," she remembers him telling her. That detail bothers me because scammers often go beyond demanding money. They prepare victims to get around the very people who might recognize that something is wrong.

Nobody stopped her

Deborah moved from location to location sending money. When I asked whether anyone challenged her or asked whether she was OK, her answer was immediate. "No. No. Not at all." By then, the scammer had already given her a cover story. He had also spent hours convincing Deborah that talking to someone could get Sarah killed.

In the end, Deborah sent $5,400 through four separate transactions using MoneyGram and Western Union. She said the transfers took all the accessible money she and her husband had. Later, she put it to me another way: "We were held hostage for 5.5 hours." Deborah and her husband could physically move, but emotionally, the caller had them exactly where he wanted them.

Deborah heard Sarah a second time

Several hours into the call, Deborah kept asking to speak with her daughter again. Eventually, the caller agreed, but even that conversation came with instructions. He told Deborah exactly what she could say: "This nightmare is nearly over. We're going to come get you as soon as we can."

Then Sarah's voice responded. "I'm so sorry, Mom. I love you." I asked Deborah again whether it really sounded like her daughter. "It was her voice," she said. "It was absolutely her voice."

Immediately afterward, another man came onto the phone. Deborah described him as an "enforcer" whose threats sounded even harsher. Soon, the scammers demanded more money.

A mother was already thinking about her daughter's life afterward

There's something Deborah later said that gives you an idea of where her mind had gone during those hours. While her husband drove and the caller listened over the phone, Deborah spent much of the trip sitting silently. Instead of wondering whether this could be a scam, her mind went to Sarah and whether she would survive it.

Deborah was already trying to figure out how her daughter would get through life after an experience like this. Paying the ransom was only part of what was running through her mind. She believed something terrible had already happened to her child and started thinking about how she would help Sarah recover afterward. That shows you how completely real this had become to her.

The caller finally says Sarah has been released

Eventually, the man told Deborah the ordeal was over. He claimed they had released Sarah outside a Walmart where Deborah and her husband were waiting. "Go get her," Deborah remembers him saying. Then he hung up.

Deborah could see the front entrance, so she got out of the car and looked for her daughter. Sarah wasn't there. For a moment, Deborah thought the criminals still had her even after taking every dollar she could reach. She frantically looked around before finally calling Sarah herself. Her daughter answered. "Hi, Mom. What's going on?" Sarah was at work.

'I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life'

For more than five hours, Deborah believed people were holding her daughter and might kill her or sell her. Then Sarah simply answered her phone from work. "I'd never been so relieved to be scammed in my life," Deborah told me.

She believes she screamed in the parking lot before the tears came. Deborah told Sarah she loved her, and after work, Sarah came to her parents' home. Her mother hugged her and sobbed. The family then went to the local police department to report what had happened. Losing the money hurt, but Sarah was alive.

Sarah immediately suspected an AI voice clone

When Deborah explained what had happened, Sarah had an immediate reaction. "Mom, that was probably an AI clone of my voice," Deborah remembers her saying. Both of Deborah's adult children work in IT, so they already knew this kind of technology existed. Deborah didn't. "I didn't know," she recalls.

Deborah firmly believes she heard an artificial intelligence-generated version of Sarah's voice. We do know the technology exists, and federal authorities have warned about criminals using it. The FTC says scammers can take a short clip of someone's real voice, including audio posted online, and use voice-cloning technology to make a call sound like that person.

How virtual kidnapping scams work

The underlying scam has been around much longer than today's AI tools. The FBI calls it "virtual kidnapping." Criminals claim they have taken someone you love even though no kidnapping occurred.

One classic warning sign closely matches Deborah's experience. The FBI says virtual kidnappers often work hard to keep victims on the phone so they can't check where their loved one actually is. The agency has also warned about ransom demands involving wire transfers to Mexico.

More recently, the FBI warned that criminals are using altered media in virtual kidnapping schemes. AI can make an old scam much more convincing. Deborah put it perfectly: "It is an old scam with new technology."

She's a Navy veteran who usually runs toward a crisis

One reaction Deborah still encounters is the question some people ask after a scam: Why didn't you hang up? Why didn't you know? Why didn't you tell someone? She understands those questions, but she also knows what was happening inside that call.

As a Navy veteran, Deborah describes herself as someone who stays calm in a crisis. "I always say I am the person that runs to the fire, not away from it." Yet the voice on the phone convinced her completely that Sarah was in danger.

That's something I want people to remember before judging anyone who falls for one of these calls. You can know about scams and handle pressure well. Then someone puts the terrified voice of your child in your ear. Criminals understand exactly what kind of emotional reaction they're trying to trigger.

The financial damage hit hard too

The $5,400 represented every readily available dollar Deborah and her husband could access. She says they are seniors living on Social Security along with income from other work, so the loss hit them hard. The following morning, Deborah went to Facebook and told her community what had happened. She also warned that criminals now had "high-tech capability."

Friends began sending money, but Deborah initially resisted because she didn't want to profit from what happened. Eventually, they convinced her to create a fundraiser on GoFundMe limited to replacing what the couple had lost. Her community raised the money back. That support couldn't erase the five-and-a-half-hour ordeal, but it meant a great deal to Deborah. Her community had shown up for her before, and they showed up again.

7 ways to protect your family from an AI voice kidnapping scam

You don't have to become an expert at detecting synthetic audio. In fact, I wouldn't build your family's defense around your ability to recognize a fake voice. A better approach is to decide now how your family will verify an emergency.

1) Call your loved one yourself

If someone claims your child, spouse or another relative has been kidnapped or injured, contact that person directly at the number you already have saved. If they don't answer, try someone who should know where they are. The FTC specifically recommends verifying the story through a phone number you know belongs to your loved one.

2) Create a private family safe word

Choose a word or phrase that someone couldn't easily discover through social media. The FBI recommends establishing a family code word for situations like virtual kidnapping scams.

Deborah also recommends a safe word now, although her experience shows why you need more than one way to verify an emergency. "There was no way I could have done any of that in this particular situation," she told me. The caller controlled when she could speak with Sarah, so don't make a safe word your family's only verification method.

3) Have another way to verify someone's location

After the scam, Deborah and Sarah began using a location-sharing app so each could see where the other was. Apple and Google also offer built-in location-sharing options. If you want to set this up on your phone, see our guide on how to share your whereabouts in any situation using your cell phone.

Location sharing comes with its own privacy considerations, so only share your location with people you trust. An agreed-upon way to check someone's whereabouts can give your family another verification tool during an emergency.

4) Pay attention when someone demands secrecy

Secrecy played a major role in Deborah's ordeal. The caller told her not to speak to anyone, listened during the transactions and gave her a fake explanation to use if someone asked questions. The FTC says urgency and secrecy are common characteristics of family emergency scams. If someone claims a loved one's survival depends on keeping you from contacting anyone else, treat that as a major warning.

5) Be extremely cautious about wire transfers

Scammers like payment methods that move money quickly and make recovery difficult. The FTC specifically warns about emergency scammers demanding wire transfers, cryptocurrency and gift cards.

If you've already sent money, contact the bank or transfer company immediately and ask whether it can stop or recall the transaction. Then report what happened to local police and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at https://t.co/Vq1B7cF2A8.

6) Reduce how much personal information criminals can find

Your name, relatives, phone numbers and other family connections can appear across people-search sites and data broker databases. That information can make a fake emergency more believable. I've tried manually removing my own information from these sites before, and keeping up with it can turn into a job because the information often returns.

A data removal service can help automate some of that work by requesting removal of your information from people-search sites and data broker databases. You can also learn more in our CyberGuy guide on removing your personal information from the web. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.

7) Talk about this scam before the phone rings

This may be the most useful conversation you have with your family this week. Tell them that a familiar voice can be faked. Agree that nobody sends emergency money until someone verifies the situation another way. A few minutes spent setting that expectation today could become extremely important when someone tries to scare you tomorrow.

Kurt's key takeaways

I've talked with a lot of scam victims over the years, and Deborah's story hit me hard. This wasn't some robotic impersonation that immediately made her suspicious. The voice sounded like her daughter having the kind of panic attack Deborah had heard before. For more than five hours, this guy kept her terrified and focused on one thing: getting Sarah home alive.

What stays with me most is where Deborah's mind went during that ordeal. Sitting in the car, she was already wondering how she would help Sarah recover from whatever these supposed kidnappers had done to her. That's a parent's mind at work. The money came later. Sarah came first.

I don't think the answer is expecting people to become experts at spotting fake audio. As the technology improves, a convincing voice could fool any of us. Instead, build another way to verify an emergency before one happens. Have a safe word, call your loved one directly and check with someone who may be physically near them. If your family feels comfortable using location sharing, set that up ahead of time.

Most importantly, talk about this with the people you love. Deborah had no idea this kind of voice scam was possible before that phone rang. Now she's sharing what happened because she doesn't want another parent sitting in a parking lot wondering whether their child is coming home. Watch or listen to my full conversation with Deborah on The CyberGuy Report podcast at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.

If you heard what sounded exactly like your child or spouse crying and begging you not to hang up, would you remember to verify the call before sending money? What does your family have in place right now? Let us know by writing to us at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.

One of the world’s oldest assets is getting a boost from America’s newest boom https://t.co/Bs1jfKqncr

Investors have long prized gold as a hedge against inflation and economic uncertainty, but one of the world’s fastest-growing industries is now fueling a new source of demand for the precious metal.

The buildout of artificial intelligence is driving investment in advanced semiconductors, servers and the sprawling data centers needed to power the technology. That expansion also requires a range of materials used in high-performance electronics, including gold.

And the AI boom is creating a growing need at a time when gold is already historically expensive. Despite those high prices, tech companies aren't necessarily switching to cheaper materials — suggesting demand for gold could continue to grow alongside AI.

A QUIET RUSH FOR GOLD IS SWEEPING THE GLOBE — HERE'S WHY COUNTRIES ARE STOCKPILING IT

Gold is valued in electronics for its conductivity, reliability and resistance to corrosion — and its role in some technology applications is proving resilient despite trading at roughly $4,153 an ounce on Oct. 6, up nearly 6%, or about $225, from a year earlier.

Joseph Cavatoni, a gold market expert and senior market strategist for North America at the World Gold Council, said companies would typically consider cheaper alternatives after developing technology that relies on gold.

But that isn't necessarily happening.

"They might pioneer a technology with gold involved and then say, ‘Let’s find something cheaper like tungsten to replace it,’" Cavatoni told Fox News Digital. "But what we’re finding in this case is they’re not."

ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

Technology demand is already showing signs of growth. Gold demand from the sector rose 2% from a year earlier to 80.4 metric tons in the second quarter, according to the World Gold Council. Electronics demand climbed 4% to 68.3 tons, fueled by AI infrastructure, high-end semiconductors and advanced components.

Cavatoni said gold can offer advantages over substitutes in applications such as chip production and heat conduction. The AI sector may also be less sensitive to elevated gold prices because relatively small amounts of the metal are needed.

"This is a rapidly growing space that’s less sensitive to price," Cavatoni said. "It’s going to likely continue to grow as the AI space grows."

Still, technology remains a small part of the overall gold market compared with investment, central-bank buying and jewelry. Cavatoni said it is "less likely to be a driver of the price of gold."

For now, Cavatoni described technology as an increasingly important contributor to gold demand that "doesn’t appear to be slowing down anytime soon."

Windows malware uses Grok AI to help stay hidden, researchers say https://t.co/ub2Vb7bDV6

A new piece of Windows malware is giving cybercriminals a lot of ways to cause trouble from one infected PC. It can steal passwords, grab browser cookies, route internet traffic through your computer and even burn through paid AI credits. Then there is the part that caught my attention. The malware, called x47.c, can reportedly use xAI's Grok to help decide how to keep itself running on an infected Windows computer.

Security researchers at Qrator Research Labs uncovered x47.c while tracking cybercrime activity. A threat actor using the name WraithTools has been advertising access to the malware, which comes with tools for stealing credentials and launching attacks. Qrator based its findings on the seller's advertisement, technical documentation, screenshots and follow-up messages, so the research shows what x47.c is advertised and designed to do rather than how widely it is currently infecting Windows PCs. Here's how it works, what the AI connection really means and the steps you can take to protect your Windows PC and accounts.

AI IS NOW POWERING CYBERATTACKS, MICROSOFT WARNS

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better health care.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.

Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.

Watch the free replays and get your checklists at https://t.co/x1SwswUebZ

How this Windows malware works

Once x47.c infects a Windows computer, the attacker can remotely control it through a management panel. Think of that infected PC as one computer in a larger network of machines controlled by the same criminal. Security researchers call that a botnet, but the important part for you is much simpler: someone else can potentially use your computer without your permission.

The operator can tell infected machines to launch online attacks. They can also steal information from those computers or use the victim's internet connection to route other traffic. Qrator found 18 advertised attack methods built into x47.c. Some can overwhelm websites and online services with traffic. Another targets something far newer: paid AI accounts.

Hackers can burn through paid AI credits

Many developers and businesses pay OpenAI, xAI and other AI companies based on how much they use their services. Access to those services often relies on a secret API key. You can think of that key as a password that lets an app communicate with an AI service and charge usage to an account.

If an attacker gets a valid API key, x47.c includes a feature that can repeatedly send requests to the AI provider. Those requests can use up prepaid credits or increase the victim's bill. Qrator describes this as a "Denial of Wallet" attack. The victim's website could keep working normally while the AI account behind part of it quietly chews through its available balance.

There is an important limit here. The attacker already needs a valid API key. x47.c does not magically break into an OpenAI or xAI account and create one. Still, that can become expensive quickly if an account allows automatic top-ups or high spending limits.

Grok can help the malware stay on your PC

The Grok connection sounds complicated, but the basic idea is pretty straightforward. Malware often tries to make sure it starts again after you reboot your computer. Security researchers call that persistence. x47.c includes what its seller calls an "AI Stealth" feature. According to Qrator, it can use Grok to look at the state of the infected computer and select from a predefined list of ways to maintain that access.

Those options include adding programs that run when Windows starts and creating scheduled tasks that can launch automatically. Grok does not appear to freely invent new attacks or control everything the malware does. Instead, it helps choose among options that the malware already has. The malware can also fall back on its own built-in methods if the AI request fails. So, cutting off its access to Grok would not necessarily remove the infection. We reached out to xAI for comment on the reported use of Grok and the safeguards it has in place to detect this kind of activity but did not hear back before our deadline.

Your saved passwords and browser sessions are targets

For most Windows users, this may be the most important part. x47.c advertises the ability to steal passwords saved in your browser. It can also collect browser cookies, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallet information and tokens tied to AI websites.

Browser cookies deserve special attention because some of them keep you signed in to websites. If malware steals an active login session, an attacker may be able to access an account without typing your password again. In some cases, changing the password alone may not immediately end a stolen session. That is why anyone dealing with an infected PC should also review active sessions and sign out of devices they do not recognize.

AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION

Your computer can also become someone else's internet connection

x47.c includes another feature called a SOCKS5 proxy. In plain English, that means a criminal can potentially route internet traffic through the infected computer. Online activity generated by the attacker could then appear to come from the victim's internet connection.

The malware's control panel lets operators see which infected computers are available to relay that traffic and whether those connections are still working. Meanwhile, the attacker can continue using the same infected machine to steal information or take part in online attacks.

9 ways to protect your Windows PC and accounts

You do not need to understand every technical feature inside x47.c to protect yourself. These steps can reduce your chances of getting infected and limit the damage if malware does reach your computer.

1) Keep Windows updated

Install Windows security updates promptly. Updates fix security weaknesses that attackers can use against PCs, even though Qrator has not identified a specific Windows vulnerability or infection method tied to x47.c. Go to Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates and install anything available.

Also remember that legitimate Windows updates come through Windows itself. A website that suddenly tells you to download a Windows update should make you suspicious. CyberGuy has previously covered fake Windows update pages that actually install malware.

2) Use strong security software

Keep strong antivirus or security software running and updated. Security tools can help catch malicious downloads and suspicious behavior before malware becomes deeply established on your computer. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at https://t.co/ExMaVpavfo.

3) Be careful about what you download

Avoid software from unfamiliar download sites, unexpected email links or pop-ups telling you that something needs an urgent update. Also be especially cautious if a webpage tells you to open Windows Run, PowerShell or Command Prompt and paste something into it. Cybercriminals increasingly use that trick to persuade people to install malware themselves. We recently covered thousands of hacked websites using fake verification prompts to push malicious Windows commands.

4) Use unique passwords

If malware steals one password, password reuse can turn one compromised account into several. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A password manager can help create and store them.

5) Turn on two-factor authentication

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible. It gives attackers another obstacle if they obtain your password. However, remember that malware capable of stealing active browser sessions creates another risk, so 2FA should be one layer of your protection rather than your only one.

HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER

6) Sign out of active sessions after an infection

If you believe your PC has been infected, changing passwords should not be your only account step. From a separate trusted device, review active login sessions for your email, financial accounts, social accounts and other important services. Sign out of unfamiliar sessions or use the service's option to sign out everywhere. Also revoke authentication tokens or connected apps you no longer recognize. Qrator specifically warns that removing the malware does not undo credentials or tokens that attackers may have already stolen.

7) Protect your AI API keys

This one mainly applies to developers, businesses and anyone paying for AI through an API. Treat an API key like a password. Never publish it in a public code repository or leave it sitting in a document that other people can access. Review AI account usage and billing for requests you do not recognize. If you think a key has leaked, revoke it and create a new one. Also use spending limits, billing alerts and controls on automatic top-ups when your AI provider offers them. Those safeguards can limit how much an attacker could spend with a stolen key.

8) Disconnect the PC if you think it has been hacked

If your computer suddenly behaves strangely or you discover malware, disconnect it from the internet. Then open your trusted security software directly and run a full scan. Do not call phone numbers in pop-ups or follow instructions from unexpected warnings on your screen. Our CyberGuy guide on what to do if your computer has been hacked walks through the next steps.

9) Change sensitive passwords from another trusted device

If malware may have stolen information from your browser, use another clean device to change the passwords for your most important accounts. Start with your primary email account because password-reset messages for other services often go there. Then move to financial accounts and other sensitive services. After changing each password, review account activity and recovery information for anything you do not recognize.

Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here isn't simply that the malware has the word AI attached to it. We've seen plenty of cyberthreats use AI as part of the sales pitch. What feels different with x47.c is how many jobs the attacker can handle from the same infected Windows PC. The malware can steal passwords and browser sessions, turn the computer into a traffic relay and help launch attacks. Then Grok can assist with choosing how the malware tries to keep its foothold on that machine. Still, the most useful lesson for you comes back to the security basics. Keep Windows updated, protect your accounts and be careful about what gets installed on your PC. And if you ever discover an infection, remember that cleaning the computer is only part of the job. You also have to assume passwords, browser sessions or other account access may already be in someone else's hands.

text:
And for those chronic GN junkies who weren’t content with the humble homage I paid to Mr. Sturke for his services to responsible journalism…and inspiring at least 1 third of my latest cyclical vlog entry..the following potted retrospective, recounted from a highly personal standpoint should sufficiently emphasise my gratitude.

Who could possibly forget his succession of equally ruthless “takedowns” carried out upon “rival” YT Tech Channel LTT, beginning with a clinical probe into the “unlimited lifetime warranty” Linus’ claimed to offer on his personally designed and “house branded” backpack.  One of many prohibitively priced “premium” products available from the channel’s perpetually promoted Online Merch Store…

Not long after, came an explosive hit piece, “ignited” by an ill-fated representative in LTT’s testing department, who dared to imply GN’s benchmark data had been accrued from “recycled results”.  GN countered by surgically analysing Linus’s own “superficial” reviews and unearthed such inconsistencies as, inexplicably favourable recommendations for Noctua’s CPU coolers, despite their performing worse than cheaper alternatives such Thermalright’s “Peerless Assassin”…or delivering results under maximum workloads that would’ve been impossible by virtue of their cooled CPU’s higher idle temperatures.  

Further damaging errata, included misquoting specs on the packaging of a certain manufacturers “combustible” power supplies, neglecting to remove the protective cellophane on the underside of a novelty mouse…thereby impeding its  optical sensor’s tracking ability…and…perhaps best of all…installing GPU coolers back to front down.  

All such petty nitpicking was a prelude to LTT’s infamous  Billet Labs Water-block Blunder…when Linus invited the referenced boutique accessory builder to provide a pre-production sample of their custom designed GPU cooler for a detailed review and performance analysis…only to then install it on a graphics card for which it wasn’t explicitly engineered…give it a resoundingly negative review…then claim his opinion wouldn’t have altered, even they’d had the “correct” card available for testing.  

This “faux-pas” was compounded when one other member LTT’s staff authorised the cooler to be raffled away as a prize at a subsequent Computex Exhibition…even though BL had specifically asked for it to be returned.  

LTT’s public apology stated that the employee had received this information too late to arrange for the bespoke cooler’s retrieval…though the date of BL’s request preceded their instructions.

Of course…this was nothing compared to the meticulous unpeeling of EK Water Block’s catastrophic cashflow crisis.  A tale of subsidiaries in a synchronised downward death spiral to insolvency…fronted by CEOs harbouring multiple conflicts of interests…and leaving countless contracted associates to shoulder material and manufacturing costs which should have been financed by the Brand’s umbrella company.  

My most recent taste of GN’s journalistic  integrity was their “feature length” dive into the deepest darkest depths of China’s Black GPU market.  A veritable docudrama apt to turn Louis Theroux’s eyes emerald with envy, and which was almost “de-platformed” due to a frivolous Copyright Claim launched by Bloomberg News for the unauthorised and use of a clip from one of President Trump’s more diplomatic speeches!!

text:
Oregon's affordable housing industrial complex is awash in billions in taxpayer money, federal tax credits, private investors...as well as serious questions surrounding lack of accountability and corruption.

And now the person who overseas the lion's share of that system (Oregon Housing and Community Services - or OHCS), is facing a serious ethics review.

OHCS executive director, Andrea Bell, failed to disclose her husband's employment with JH Brawner, a consulting firm involved in the multiple affordable housing projects that received 10's of millions of dollars from her agency.

Bell only amended her financial disclosures once reporters began asking her questions.

But there's an even bigger story here:

OHSC has distributed more than $1.4 billion in state housing subsidies over five years. That doesn't include the enormous value of federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC) allocated through the agency.

Here's how LIHTC works: Developers receive allocations of federal tax credits, which are then sold to private investors in exchange for capital. Investors then receive federal tax benefits over ten years, while developers receive financing for projects.

It's an incredibly complex system that brings together government agencies (such as OHCS), private developers (such as Community Development Partners - or CDP), banks and financial institutions, and large investment firms. And the public deserves to know exactly where the money goes.

Nearly two years ago, we investigated Milepost 5, a Portland affordable housing complex that had descended into deplorable conditions (as affordable housing properties tend to do) despite millions in public subsidies and tax-credit financing.

Our investigation revealed that the investment entity CDP, a private California company that develops many affordable housing projects in the Portland-metro area, is a subsidiary of Aegon Group, an international hedge fund worth north of $300 billion.

Although OHCS awarded CDP $3.3 million for upgrades and repairs at Milepost 5, serious maintenance problems persisted, along with drug dealing, squatters, and repeated complaints from residents and neighbors. At one point, there was even a raid by Homeland Security Investigations at the property, in which they arrested multiple drug dealers who had taken up residence in the building.

CDP claimed that seismic upgrades consumed most of the $3.3 million, despite an earlier estimate of approximately $350,000 for the seismic work. According to CDP, this left insufficient funding to address many of the property's other problems.

After contacting multiple people within CDP, OHCS, and local government, we were unable to obtain a satisfactory accounting of exactly how the $3.3 million was spent. Everyone involved just wanted the questions about the funds to go away.

In fact, a local whistleblower who lives near Milepost 5 was threatened with arrest after U.S. Senator Jeff Merkley’s office allegedly identified him as a man who had been behaving threateningly outside the senator’s office. There was just one problem: the whistleblower was out of town on a fishing trip at the time, and the man in question bore no resemblance to him. Nevertheless, the accusation reportedly led to an attempt to have the whistleblower arrested. Even after the mistaken identity was established, neither Merkley nor his office offered the whistleblower an apology. Senator Merkley needs to answer to this egregious behavior. 

While OHCS did publicly admonish CDP for its failures at Milepost 5 at a meeting, two weeks later, the agency approved $43.6 million to CDP for the Julia West affordable housing project. 

In a news story by ProPublica (see below) the publication exposed how Oregon law shields detailed financial information about subsidized housing developments from public scrutiny. 

There are billions in state subsidies. Federal tax credits benefitting private investors. Complex ownership structures. Limited public access to financial records.

And now an ethics review involving the director of the agency responsible for overseeing much of it.

Both the Bell controversy and Milepost 5 raise fundamental questions about oversight, transparency, and whose interests Oregon's affordable housing system is actually serving. 

Because it doesn't seem to serve the people who are unfortunate enough to have to live in places like Milepost 5 or any of the other dozens of affordable housing projects in this city that are constantly falling into disrepair. It seems to mostly serve out of state corporations and huge international hedge funds.

The state (i.e. Gov. Kotek) and local government tell us that affordable housing should be about providing safe, stable homes for the people who really need them - not for moving enormous sums of public money through an increasingly complicated financial industrial complex, one that appears to be rife with corruption.

Below are the articles from ProPublica and our article about Milepost 5.

text:
PART II: Months of double dealing and deliberate misrepresentation preceded the first shot at Sumter—none of which PragerU bothers to mention. Buchanan gave South Carolina an informal pledge to preserve the status quo in Charleston Harbor and not move troops from Fort Moultrie. When Anderson shifted his garrison to Sumter on the night of December 26, SC negotiators were appalled. Secretary of War John B. Floyd, who had favored a hands-off policy, resigned, saying the distrust could only lead to war, as Federal assurances were now meaningless.

The pattern continued under Lincoln. Governor Pickens granted Gustavus Fox access to Sumter after Fox assured him the visit was for peaceful purposes connected to possible abandonment; Fox returned with a detailed assessment of the garrison’s supplies and the feasibility of a night relief. Ward Hill Lamon, Lincoln’s personal friend and special agent, was likewise allowed to meet Anderson and Pickens under diplomatic cover and left both with the clear impression that evacuation was imminent. Lincoln himself was reported to have told William Cabell Rives that if Virginia stayed in the Union he would abandon Sumter—an offer later echoed in talks with Virginia convention delegates. Seward spent weeks privately signaling Confederate commissioners that the fort would be given up, while Alexander Stephens publicly stated on March 21 in his so-called "Cornerstone Speech" that Sumter would soon be abandoned.  

No record shows Lincoln was unaware of Seward’s contacts, and the cumulative effect of these conflicting assurances left Governor Pickens with no reliable way to judge whether the April notice of “provisions only” meant food or the opening of a reinforcement effort. PragerU’s video erases every one of these steps and then presents the bombardment as an unprompted Confederate choice rather than the product of repeated broken understandings.

Now do you see why they want to pretend 3 months didn't exist?

text:
Teapot

茶壶——美国波士顿1740年左右

这件茶壶由18世纪美国银匠雅各布·赫德（Jacob Hurd，1702–1758）打造，是马萨诸塞州波士顿手工银器的代表作之一。整体尺寸为高14.8厘米，长22.6厘米（含把手），仅壶身高12.6厘米。茶壶采用纯银制成，展现了当时波士顿银匠精湛的锻造技巧和对细节的严格把控。

银质表面光洁，形态稳重而优雅，造型设计典雅实用。壶顶配有一个宝珠状的钮，但据记录该钮可能不是原配，后期更换的可能性较大。细观壶身，铭刻有惠普尔（Whipple）家族的纹章，强调了身份和所有权，这种刻章不仅是装饰手法，也是当时工艺品归属的权威标识。

茶壶的制作时期正值18世纪中叶，恰逢新兴的美洲殖民地社会逐渐形成独特的文化身份，银器不仅作为日用器皿，也体现了主人的社会地位和身份认同。雅各布·赫德是当时波士顿著名银匠，这只茶壶也因此承载了丰富的历史背景和工艺传统。

观赏时应注意壶体的比例和线条流畅度，银器的光泽和雕刻细节，尤其是徽章部分的精细雕琢。此外，壶钮的非原装状态提醒我们关注文物的保护和时代更迭给物品带来的变化。

此茶壶由J. H. Wade赠予博物馆，曾为Lawrence Park所有，收藏历史为其增添了展品的文化价值。总体而言，通过这件银器，我们得以窥见18世纪美国殖民地社会的生活气息及工匠的匠心独运，展现了一段历史与艺术交织的篇章。

Teapot circa 1740, Boston, Massachusetts

This silver teapot was crafted around 1740 by Jacob Hurd (1702–1758), a prominent American silversmith based in Boston, Massachusetts. Measuring 14.8 cm in height and 22.6 cm in length including the handle, with the body alone at 12.6 cm tall, it exemplifies mid-18th-century colonial American silverwork. The teapot is made entirely of silver, reflecting the refined techniques and careful workmanship characteristic of Hurd's studio.

The piece exhibits a balanced and elegant form, maintaining both aesthetic refinement and practical design. Notably, the finial atop the lid is likely a later addition and not original to the teapot, which speaks to the historical process of alteration and preservation in such objects. Engraved on the body is the coat of arms of the Whipple family, a clear marker of identity and ownership. This heraldic engraving functions both as decorative art and as an authoritative signifier of provenance, common in silverware of the period.

The teapot dates from a formative period in American colonial society when objects like silverware symbolized more than utilitarian use: they communicated social status and personal identity within the community. Jacob Hurd was a well-known Boston silversmith, and pieces from his hand often carry significant cultural and historical weight. This teapot, with its precise construction and detailed embellishment, offers insight into the material culture and craftsmanship of the time.

When examining the teapot, attention should be given to the overall proportions and smooth flow of its lines, the reflective surface of the silver, and particularly to the finely executed coat of arms engraving. The non-original finial invites contemplation of the object's changing history and the impact of conservation decisions.

The teapot entered the museum collection as a gift from J. H. Wade and was previously owned by Lawrence Park, adding layers to its documented ownership history. Through this single piece, viewers gain a tangible connection to 18th-century colonial life and the artisanal skill embodied in early American decorative arts, underscoring the intertwined narrative of identity, craftsmanship, and historical context.

🇸🇻₿🤖BITCOIN & AI: EL SALVADOR WEEKLY — VOL. 9

FRIDAY, OCTOBER 9, 2026

THE PEOPLE, PROJECTS & IDEAS SHAPING WHAT'S NEXT

This week, El Salvador's publicly reported Bitcoin treasury crossed another milestone, a collaboration between the Bitcoin Office and the Ministry of Agriculture brought Texas cattle genetics to the country, and Salvadoran students explored the technologies behind Bitcoin and artificial intelligence.

Meanwhile, a Salvadoran robotics researcher received recognition for his scientific publication record, and El Salvador's AI strategy reached an international audience in San Francisco.

From Bitcoin reserves to cattle breeding, from computer science to robotics, this week's developments illustrate the range of projects taking shape across El Salvador.

🇸🇻₿ 1. EL SALVADOR'S BITCOIN TREASURY CROSSES 7,800 BTC

A NEW MILESTONE FOR THE NATIONAL BITCOIN RESERVE

El Salvador's publicly reported Bitcoin holdings reached a new milestone on Friday, October 9.

According to a screenshot of the National Bitcoin Office's official treasury dashboard circulated by Bitcoin Magazine and reposted by the Bitcoin Office, the country's holdings reached approximately 7,800.37 BTC.

The milestone follows the 7,792.37 BTC balance recorded in our previous weekly report on October 2.

That represents an increase of approximately eight Bitcoin in seven days.

The dashboard's balance-history chart continues to show a rising treasury balance, a development that has attracted attention from international Bitcoin publications.

The Bitcoin Office also reposted commentary celebrating El Salvador's continued Bitcoin accumulation.

The latest figures offer another chapter in a national Bitcoin story that began with the country's adoption of Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 and continues to attract international attention.

7,800 BTC AND COUNTING. 🇸🇻₿

🐂₿ 2. FROM TEXAS TO EL SALVADOR: THE ARRIVAL OF BITCOIN BEEFSTEAK

BITCOIN OFFICE AND MAG COLLABORATE ON LIVESTOCK GENETICS

One of the week's most unexpected Bitcoin-related stories came from El Salvador's agricultural sector.

The Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAG), working with the National Bitcoin Office, announced the addition of two Santa Gertrudis breeding bulls to support efforts to improve the country's cattle genetics.

One of the animals was imported from Texas, United States.

Vice Minister of Agriculture and Livestock Óscar Domínguez explained that the breeding program is intended to improve the genetic quality of Salvadoran cattle herds.

“These bulls are and will be the fathers of thousands of calves throughout the country,” Domínguez stated.

The broader MAG reproductive program includes several cattle breeds, among them Senepol, Brown Swiss, Girolando, Brahman and Angus.

The ministry also offers semen doses to livestock producers starting at $2.83, making genetic improvement services available through its animal reproduction facilities.

A WELCOME AT THE AIRPORT

Bitcoin Office Director Stacy Herbert shared photographs of the arrival of the Santa Gertrudis bulls from Texas.

The images showed a group welcoming the animals at the airport, including Herbert and Max Keiser.

The Bitcoin Office celebrated the initiative with a distinctly Bitcoin-flavored message:

“Better genetics, better beef.”

And then came the line that gave the story its name:

“The era of Bitcoin Beefsteak has arrived.”

The collaboration highlights the Bitcoin Office's participation in an initiative beyond the digital-asset sector, connecting its international network with a practical agricultural development project.

For Salvadoran cattle producers, the objective is straightforward: better genetics and improved breeding opportunities.

FROM TEXAS RANCHES TO SALVADORAN FARMS. 🇸🇻🐂

₿🎓 3. CUBO+ TAKES STUDENTS DOWN THE BITCOIN RABBIT HOLE

TOM TABER EXPLORES THE TECHNOLOGY AND IDEAS BEHIND BITCOIN

On October 8, Bitcoin educator and Montaña Sagrada co-founder Tom Taber delivered a special class to CUBO+ students in San Salvador.

The session, titled “Bitcoin Rabbit Holes,” explored aspects of Bitcoin extending beyond its market price.

According to CUBO+, the discussion examined Bitcoin's technological foundations, its influence on society and its potential implications for El Salvador's future.

Photographs from the classroom showed students working on laptops while Taber discussed topics including monetary systems, computer science, cryptography and game theory.

Before the session, Taber described the opportunity to speak with Salvadoran students as a privilege.

He praised the country's Bitcoin community and expressed enthusiasm about sharing his knowledge with students he described as future leaders.

CUBO+ subsequently confirmed that the class had taken place, publishing photographs of the session and thanking Taber for his participation.

The class illustrates an important part of El Salvador's Bitcoin education ecosystem: exposure to experienced international educators and the opportunity to examine the technology from multiple disciplines.

BEYOND THE PRICE. BEHIND THE PROTOCOL. INTO THE FUTURE. ₿

🤖💻 4. FROM MACHINE LEARNING TO AI AGENTS: CUBO AI STUDENTS BUILD WHAT COMES NEXT

TWO HANDS-ON LEARNING EXPERIENCES IN ONE WEEK

El Salvador's AI education ecosystem continued moving forward this week as CUBO AI students participated in practical sessions covering machine learning fundamentals and AI-powered workflows.

OCTOBER 4 — UNDERSTANDING HOW MACHINES LEARN

Instructor Camila Cruz, working with CUBO AI and C2 Labs AI, led a class focused on machine learning from first principles.

Students explored mathematical foundations, built basic algorithms, trained a model and observed it generating predictions.

The session also introduced the perceptron, a foundational building block of neural networks.

By examining weights, biases and activation functions, participants explored how mathematical operations help machine-learning models process information.

The emphasis was on understanding the technology rather than simply using ready-made AI tools.

OCTOBER 9 — PUTTING AI AGENTS TO WORK

On Friday, CUBO AI continued its hands-on training with a workshop focused on Fluso, an AI workspace designed to support automated workflows.

Instructors Moisés Iglesias and Rodrigo Trujillo guided students through the platform, examining how AI agents can assist with practical tasks.

According to CUBO AI's posts, participants compared Fluso's features with other AI tools before working directly with the platform.

The two sessions illustrated complementary skills: understanding how machine learning operates and learning how AI-powered systems can be applied to real workflows.

For Salvadoran students preparing to enter a technology-driven economy, both are relevant areas of technical education.

FIRST, LEARN HOW AI WORKS. THEN, LEARN HOW TO BUILD WITH IT. 🇸🇻🤖

🏆🤖 5. ANIA HIGHLIGHTS SALVADORAN ROBOTICS RESEARCHER'S SCIENTIFIC MILESTONE

DR. MANUEL CARDONA RECORDS 141 SCOPUS-INDEXED PUBLICATIONS

El Salvador's National Artificial Intelligence Agency (ANIA) recognized a scientific publication milestone involving one of its strategic advisers.

On October 6, ANIA congratulated Dr. Manuel Cardona after he appeared first in a ranking of ten Salvadoran researchers by number of Scopus-indexed publications.

According to the ranking shared by Cardona, using figures dated September 30, 2026, the researcher had accumulated 141 indexed publications.

The ten researchers included in the ranking accounted for a combined 449 publications.

Cardona, affiliated with STEAM Robotics Academy, represented approximately 31.4% of that total.

His research includes kinematics, mechatronics and autonomous systems—disciplines closely connected to robotics and the emerging field of physical AI.

THE RESEARCH ECOSYSTEM BEHIND THE NUMBERS

The ranking also highlighted the contribution of Salvadoran universities.

The University of El Salvador placed six researchers among the ten listed, accounting for 221 publications.

The Technological University of El Salvador contributed two researchers, while the Central American University José Simeón Cañas had one.

Cardona's position drew attention to STEAM Robotics Academy's growing involvement in scientific research alongside its educational activities.

The ranking measures publication volume, rather than research quality or impact, but it provides a useful snapshot of scientific activity across Salvadoran institutions.

For ANIA, the recognition also highlights the research experience represented within its advisory network.

141 PUBLICATIONS. ROBOTICS. AUTONOMOUS SYSTEMS. SALVADORAN SCIENTIFIC TALENT. 🇸🇻🔬

🌎🤖 6. EL SALVADOR'S AI STRATEGY REACHES SAN FRANCISCO TECH WEEK

GINGER LUCKEY GAETZ PRESENTS EL SALVADOR'S APPROACH TO EMERGING TECHNOLOGY

El Salvador also appeared in international AI discussions this week during San Francisco Tech Week.

On October 6, ANIA shared footage of strategic adviser Ginger Luckey Gaetz participating in a technology panel and discussing El Salvador's approach to artificial intelligence.

The agency emphasized its preference for innovation-friendly frameworks and opportunities for emerging technologies.

Gaetz's participation connected El Salvador's national AI ambitions with a broader international discussion involving technology founders, investors and industry specialists.

El Salvador on X covered the development in a standalone article on October 7.

The appearance complements the country's domestic AI education initiatives, bringing international engagement and local talent development into the same weekly picture.

EL SALVADOR'S AI CONVERSATION IS TAKING PLACE AT HOME AND ABROAD. 🇸🇻🌎

🇸🇻 THE WEEK IN NUMBERS

Bitcoin treasury — Approximately 7,800.37 BTC reported October 9

Agricultural genetics — 2 Santa Gertrudis bulls added through MAG–Bitcoin Office collaboration

Livestock breeding — Semen doses available from $2.83

Bitcoin education — Tom Taber's October 8 CUBO+ class

AI education — 2 learning activities covering machine learning and AI workflows

Scientific research — 141 Scopus-indexed publications reported for Dr. Manuel Cardona

International AI — ANIA adviser participates in San Francisco Tech Week

🇸🇻 THE BIGGER PICTURE

This week's stories connect several areas of El Salvador's development.

The national Bitcoin treasury reached a newly reported milestone. @bitcoinofficesv participated in an agricultural genetics initiative. @cuboplus students examined Bitcoin's technological foundations, while @cubo_ai students worked with machine-learning concepts and AI agents.

At the research level, Dr. @ManuelCardona_'s publication record drew attention to Salvadoran scientific work in robotics and autonomous systems.

And internationally, El Salvador's AI strategy was part of the conversation in San Francisco.

These developments range from established financial technology to emerging applications in agriculture, education and research.

BITCOIN. ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE. EDUCATION. INNOVATION.

EL SALVADOR IS BUILDING ACROSS MULTIPLE FRONTS. 🇸🇻₿🤖

text:
i don't generally support the death penalty* and i think his views are wrong here. 

he did often take some logical endpoint then frame it in the way that would be the most jarring and objectionable, which loses a lot of people

i believe what he is getting at is that there cannot be a punishment with infinite process in front of it, because then that punishment doesn't actually exist, the maximum punishment is just endless process, which seems kafkaesque

and i think at the core of that it is correct. and then the next pivotal step is to realize, huh, yeah, we can't erect a sufficient process around this punishment so we shouldn't bother with it. and we don't need it. and he failed to get that far.

but he wasn't just saying "let's kill poor defendants because i don't like them." and we know this because he was often the first to say the state can't take shortcuts to punish criminal defendants. and separately because of cases, like Texas v. Johnson, where he voted for communists he openly despised, but voted for them anyway because he believed the constitution was with them

he was also saying the better remedy for this is executive clemency or amending the law, because those both offer an independent source of morality and a source of finality that "endless court process" cannot provide

* except in maybe a few extremely exceptional cases

text:
SpaceXAI just shipped two of the biggest Grok Build CLI updates back to back

An absolute powerhouse release packed with background workflow controls, zero-leak secure credential forms, persistent Chrome profiles, live skill completions, native Jujutsu support, and a massive wave of stability fixes

@grok Build updated to 1.0.51

Breaking Changes:

• Cancel and edit-resend on long sessions no longer unexpectedly revert workspace files

• Memory settings simplified: rollout and file_writes_enabled options removed; memory is on or off

• Removed the /share command and related session sharing features from the CLI and SDK

Features:

• Inline viewports can now be restored at a previously saved screen area without extra cursor queries

• Headless grok -p now waits for background goals to finish and reports their outcome

• /imagine and similar commands now run the matching bundled skill when the required tools are unavailable

• New /density command and Tool call density setting let you choose how much detail tool calls show in the transcript

• Web fetch approval cards now include "always allow" and "never allow" domain options that persist for the folder

• Slash command completion now updates live when skills are added or changed during a session

• Request form now securely collects and fills sensitive details like passwords or card numbers without sending values to the model

• Chrome profiles can now be persisted across restarts using durable state directories

• Workspace server sessions now share one Chrome instance for cookies and storage

• /feedback Drafts tab now supports G / Home and End to jump to the first or last draft

• Pinned sessions on the dashboard now stay in the order you pinned or reordered them

• Shift+Enter, Ctrl+., Ctrl+/ and Ctrl+[ / ] now work inside tmux when extended-keys are enabled

• grok -p --output-format json now reports the exact worktree folder used (useful after -w name collisions)

• Bare hook commands such as my-guard now run from PATH when not found next to the hook file

• Headless JSON error output now includes the worktree folder when a session was started

• grok sessions list and /resume now show worktree sessions started from the same subfolder

• /exit (and aliases) in a dashboard details view now closes only that session instead of quitting Grok

• Editors offering file access now receive a one-time transcript notice that the agent reads and writes disk files

• --background-wait-timeout now also stops an active headless goal after the timeout and exits with an error

• Interactive sessions now include the Grok Build user guide location so the agent can answer usage questions

• New /workflow commands let you list, stop, and resume background workflow runs without sending them to the model

• Background workflow runs now appear in the tasks pane with a stop button

• Hooks that ask about web searches or file deletes now show the hook name on the approval card

• config.toml now accepts an [update] section without breaking other commands

• Hook load errors listed in /hooks can now be expanded to see the full message

• grok worktree commands now work correctly inside Jujutsu repositories

• Images pasted with skill commands like /pr-workflow are now sent to the model

• Pressing Ctrl+C on a goal now pauses the goal instead of letting it continue

• grok -p now runs auth_provider_command when no login is stored

• Reopening a chat with an active goal now continues the goal automatically

• Browser tabs can now be restored on demand instead of all at once when a session resumes

• grok agent stdio now supports listing sessions via ACP and returns consistent reply envelopes

• Answering an approval with a message now tells the model it is a follow-up

• --allowed-tools is now accepted as an alias for --allow in headless mode

Bug Fixes:

• Slash command suggestions no longer make the text after the cursor disappear while typing

• Running workflows in the dock now show the same pulsing indicator as in the main scrollback

• Mode switch tool calls now appear in the transcript with the target mode name

• Always-approve mode now automatically approves web requests without extra prompts

• The follow indicator no longer appears when only blank padding sits below the viewport

• Search failures now keep the original pattern instead of showing an empty Search ""

• Sessions that open without a model list now use the public Auto id and succeed on every account

• Background wake turns that request plan changes or mode switches are now handled correctly

• Model-call retries now show progress status instead of a generic waiting message

• Foreground subagent activity now appears correctly after resume

• Very large pasted prompts are now offloaded to a file instead of being sent inline

• Sign-in failures now show a clear plain-English message with the next step instead of raw errors

• Logging out now stops any running turns on local sessions instead of leaving them active

• The send-now shortcut no longer accidentally enables always-approve mode while a permission card is open

• /find now keeps match counts and navigation accurate while replies or command output stream in

• Images from tools are now validated so bad files no longer break the current turn or future replays

• Screenshots and other image artifacts saved by the browser tool are now stored as real image files

• Rate-limit errors now show the expected message; very small images are rejected early

• Send-now (Ctrl+Enter) no longer accidentally answers an open question card

• Opening the queue with Up now scrolls so the selected follow-up is visible

• Command output that contains clear-screen codes is no longer discarded

• Dashboard cursor and overlay counter now correctly track the active grouping view

• Headless JSON output now reports the correct stop reason when the turn limit is reached and removes duplicate error prefixes

• Session picker footer no longer lists the same shortcut twice

• Dragging images from a file manager onto terminals like GNOME Terminal or xfce4-terminal now attaches them correctly

• Plan comments added while a revision runs are now preserved and sent when the plan is approved

• Permission prompts that fail now show a clearer message without blaming the interface

• --disallowed-tools now accepts the exact names shown to the model (run_terminal_command, spawn_subagent, etc.)

• Long pastes without bracketed-paste markers are now read completely instead of stalling after ~1 KB

• A feedback send now shows "Sending feedback..." immediately; failed sends no longer repeat the lead phrase

• Typing, arrows or Enter while an approval card appears no longer accidentally approve the action or enable always-approve mode

• Error hints for legacy session import now appear in full instead of being cut off by the pager

• Skills in the folder where grok started now correctly show as (local)

• Worktree creation no longer hangs when the repo contains named pipes or sockets

• --no-subagents flag now works correctly in headless / -p sessions

• Resumed sessions now correctly show aborted subagent tasks as cancelled instead of failed

• Large parallel shell batches no longer drop calls with "hook state lost" errors

• Write approval cards now show the existing file contents that will be replaced

• Slash command completion now shows the correct name for files under commands/ instead of always showing /commands

• PreToolUse hooks now validate rewrites against the tool schema and deny invalid ones before running the tool

• Ctrl+C during a turn now cancels the turn even when a modal such as /mcps or the block viewer is open

• grok -w now opens the session at the worktree root (with a note) when the original launch folder does not exist in the new worktree

• /cd and the location picker now accept quoted or escaped folder paths

• PreToolUse hooks for shell commands now see the model's block_until_ms value

• MCP tool calls now show hook permission prompts and cards name the hook that asked

• Typing while a permission or ask card is visible no longer selects or answers the card

• grok worktree list now shows unfinished copies left by an interrupted create

• Auto mode now asks before deleting files that the classifier has not already allowed

• Fixed intermittent List/Read/Open failures during concurrent v2 hardening migrations

• grok -p -s with a reused session id now shows the plain refusal message instead of JSON-RPC noise

• Settings saves no longer re-insert the built-in default fork model into config.toml

• Fixed several pager rows that showed wrong paths, truncated names, or hid failure/cancel states

• --system-prompt now correctly appends rules from --append-system-prompt instead of dropping them

• /new now inherits always-approve mode from the tab it was run from instead of another tab

• Multi-select questions now let you toggle several answers with number keys before submitting

• Slash-command notices typed while a reply streams no longer hide the streaming reply

• @ file search no longer accepts keys or moves the highlight while results are still updating

• Worktree db rebuild now restores names so rm and show by name work again

• A prompt blocked by a hook no longer titles the session

• Background subagents now respect saved approvals and --always-approve after the parent turn finishes

• Per-session system prompt overrides now correctly use only the session's own rules

• Connection stalled errors now show a clearer message with network advice

• Invalid model provider tables now produce a clear startup error instead of silent fallback

• Narrow feedback dialog now shows full draft titles and readable confirm prompts

• /workflow stop|resume <name> now correctly targets the live run instead of an ended first run

• Dialogs like /feedback no longer disappear on very short terminal windows

• Delete operations now respect the same permission rules as shell rm commands

• Hooks can no longer rewrite a web-search call to restrict domains

• Workspace server now starts with per-session private Chrome by default

• Notification hooks for permission prompts and task completion now run reliably before a headless session exits

• Headless goal runs no longer print a spurious "Goal paused" message after completion

• Legacy UI density settings now combine correctly across config tiers and produce expected folding

• Approval answers sent after a turn ends no longer affect the turn

• Background shell commands now fail immediately when the working directory does not exist

• grok worktree rm without -f now safely keeps worktrees when the unsaved-work check fails or times out

• The dashboard slash menu now shows skills from the home session even when opened early

• grok worktree rm and gc now correctly remove worktrees whose only untracked content is empty folders

• Editing a queued prompt now prevents accidental removal with a stale client view

• The model is now told when memory is turned off or on for the session

• Hook results in the UI now correctly distinguish between notes and tool outcomes

• Permission cards for MCP tools can no longer be tricked into showing fake option rows

• The agent stdio mode now returns clearer errors for malformed client requests and consistent recap replies

• Scroll logging and acceleration calculations no longer produce backwards timestamps under load

• Hooks and tool commands started from the TUI can no longer read or write the interactive terminal

• Delete operations now correctly match Bash(rm ...) ask/deny rules even when the path contains .. or the cwd is a symlink

• Web search and image approval cards now only offer always-approve mode to clients that support it

• Closing a session in the dashboard no longer leaves it listed under Inactive

• Running /compact on an empty session no longer resets the reported context window

• With goals disabled, a headless /goal line is now treated as a normal prompt instead of failing

• Background shell commands no longer flip back to running when late output arrives

• Only slash commands at the start of a message trigger skills

• Browser tabs restore and close more reliably with fewer races

• Fast model names in the footer no longer show double parentheses

• SubagentStart and Notification hook activity is no longer reported to the UI

• Voice error messages now display with correct punctuation

• disable_zdr_incompatible_tools changes now apply to new turns without restarting the worker

• Project skills are now labeled correctly for nested projects

Performance:

• Opening the resume picker is now much faster on machines with many worktrees

• grok worktree commands start faster by skipping unnecessary model catalog work at boot

text:
Grok Build just dropped a massive update featuring stricter worktree safety checks, compact mode improvements, interactive spreadsheet table export buttons, and deep session management refinements

@grok Build updated to 1.0.50

Breaking Changes:

• grok worktree rm without -f now refuses to delete worktrees that are in use or contain unsaved changes and exits with an error

Features:

• Compact mode now collapses recaps and keeps inner spacing on tall terminals

• Clicking the git branch in the header now copies the full branch name

• Long branch names now abbreviate on narrow terminals while remaining copyable

• Targeted cancels now stop only the specific response when requested by clients

• Compact mode now hides the dock (or tasks pane) the same way Ctrl+G does

• New timestamps setting offers off, minimal, and on modes in Settings and /timestamps

• Shell command output now shows "Running ..." while executing and "Ran ..." when finished

• Live preview pins now include whether an app was observed behind the URL

• Command palette (Ctrl+P) and model picker now open at the same width as the settings modal

• Tables rendered by grok now show copy buttons underneath that export clean TSV, CSV or Markdown suitable for spreadsheets

• Dashboard now shows which worktree each session belongs to, displays the -m model in the new-agent box, and lets you toggle worktree mode in the folder picker

Bug Fixes:

• Shell permission decisions now correctly prompt or approve commands matching the permission manager

• Cancelled turns now correctly mark unanswered tool calls as cancelled instead of succeeded

• Long error messages in the /usage and /session-info modals now wrap instead of being truncated

• Em-dashes no longer appear in status messages and subagent rows

• Stalled model calls during turns now retry before failing the turn

• Queue pane and Ctrl+; now appear and work when the dock is hidden with Ctrl+G

• Long sessions no longer disconnect when the conversation exceeds 4 MiB

• Permission rules now accept native tool names such as run_terminal_command and Shell

• /rewind now places the cursor at the end of the restored prompt

• Failed file writes now leave the previous contents instead of an empty file

• Fixed /loop and scheduler_create so non-ASCII intervals like 5分 no longer crash the session

• Fixed --disallowed-tools when only one scheduler tool is named; the other two no longer cause startup failure

• Fixed closing a busy tab so queued prompts are no longer sent to the model

• Fixed relative --cwd so grok --cwd a no longer ends up running inside a/a

• The terminal title now shows "Action Required" for any background session waiting on approval

• grok now accepts a prompt via piped stdin in headless mode instead of trying to open the UI

• An admin-set [features] title_refresh = false in requirements.toml now correctly disables title refresh even when GROK_TITLE_REFRESH is set

• Custom notification commands defined under [[ui.notifications.hooks]] now execute on matching events

• An admin pin of [cli] use_leader = false now correctly prevents --leader from starting a leader process

• When multiple MCP servers expose a tool with the same name, search_tool now returns all of them

• Concurrent Grok windows editing settings no longer lose or corrupt config.toml entries such as MCP servers or permission rules

• web_fetch no longer downloads huge files into memory before rejecting them

• memory_get no longer returns huge files that exceed the read limit

• Continue to run no longer kills commands running inside background subagents

• memory_search now finds Japanese, Chinese, and Korean words inside longer notes

• Drafts saved by the model now appear under their actual titles in /feedback

• Imagine replies that are not valid images are now rejected instead of being saved as .jpg files

• A workflow file that fails to parse now reports the exact file and parse error instead of 'unknown workflow'

• Re-encoded images are now oriented correctly using their EXIF tags instead of appearing sideways

• Image and log paths reported after /fork --worktree now point to real files instead of missing locations

• Tab characters in terminal command output are now preserved when shown to the model

• Transparent images are now kept as PNG when re-encoded instead of turning black

• The bundled ripgrep is now available to terminal commands even on images that do not install it

• Request bodies now stay under a small configured max_request_bytes limit instead of growing past it

• Effort level now stays the same after a bare /model switch instead of jumping to the new model's default

• *Ctrl+\* and other modified digits no longer accidentally select options on permission or cancel cards

• Feedback submissions now show accurate success or failure messages without premature thanks or duplicated prefixes

• grok doctor now reports the exact config file or setting that prevents Grok from starting instead of saying zero issues

• Recap summaries now appear on screen automatically instead of requiring manual scrolling

• grok doctor fix now opens its confirmation card on Cancel to prevent accidental edits to shell or tmux config

• Slash commands now run regardless of case (e.g. /COMPACT or /Compact)

• /context no longer shows an invented auto-compact threshold when the agent does not report one

• Agent text no longer keeps the pager redrawing when a tool call interrupts the sentence

• CLI tool calls no longer fail or overflow when the workspace directory is deleted or output is huge

• Logs written to files or when NO_COLOR is set are now plain text instead of containing color codes

• Prompts now fail immediately with a clear message if the session's working directory no longer exists instead of failing later or recreating it

• grok -w now works correctly with separate-git-dir repositories and shows clear errors when run outside a git repo or on an empty repo

• Shell tool descriptions now correctly state the actual output truncation limit, and grep respects globs relative to the current session directory

• Compaction messages now scroll into view instead of appearing below the bottom of the screen after a turn finishes

• Git-mode worktrees created with -w now preserve uncommitted changes instead of dropping them

• Worktrees created with --worktree-ref no longer contain wrong submodule contents or LFS pointer text

• Worktree creation now shows the same clear error messages on every code path

• Failed worktree creates now show a clear error on the home screen instead of being hidden

• Merge and rebase conflicts now appear in the changes list instead of being hidden

• Fixed a crash when starting a new session with durable rewind checkpoints enabled

• Managed permission files with one bad key no longer lose all their valid rules

• Simultaneous worktree creates with the same label now succeed instead of one failing with "already exists"

• grok worktree rm without -f no longer deletes arbitrary folders that happen to share a name with a removed worktree

• Discard now affects only the exact files you select instead of also deleting or reverting similarly-named files

• Permission rules with one bad entry no longer lose the other rules in the same section

• Chat Completions streams that end without a finish reason are now retried instead of returning partial output

• grok worktree rm by label now refuses when the label exists in multiple repos

• Grep now respects Read deny rules that use a leading ./

Performance:

• Command hooks no longer cause large memory spikes when they print a lot of output
• Retry waits now vary between processes instead of being identical

ANOTHER MARYLAND BREWERY FACES CLOSURE: BLACK FLAG BREWING COULD SHUT DOWN NOVEMBER 30 AFTER 10 YEARS IN COLUMBIA.

COLUMBIA, Md. — Another popular Maryland brewery could soon close its doors.

Black Flag Brewing Company, a fixture at 9315 Snowden River Parkway for a decade, faces a possible November 30 closure as efforts to sell the business encounter financing problems.

Founder Brian Gaylor says he decided to sell after the birth of his first child, recognizing he could no longer devote the time needed to operate the brewery.

A prospective buyer — another Maryland-based brewing company — has struggled to secure financing, putting the agreement and the brewery’s future in jeopardy.

Gaylor is now entertaining additional offers in hopes of keeping Black Flag operating and preserving employees’ jobs.

The news comes just days after Guinness announced plans to close its Open Gate Brewery in Halethorpe, another major loss for Maryland’s brewing industry.

Brewers across the state are confronting rising operating costs, changing consumer habits and declining alcohol consumption.

Black Flag has not officially closed. November 30 is the potential final day if a sale or alternative arrangement cannot be completed.
