Wally Odum: Don’t Let Religion Steal Your Joy
A Grace Grenade Original Message
I’ve been in church all my life. I consider that a great blessing. My parents led me to a relationship with Jesus when I was a child. As an adult, I have been a pastor and teacher for more years than I care to remember. Over those years I have seen too many come to Christ with great joy because they have encountered God’s grace, then lose their joy. Man-made religion makes an inroad into that relationship and they struggle to live out their faith in their own strength. Too often they become frustrated and give up. That condition is easily identified. It is their loss of joy. That progression happened in New Testament days, too. Paul wrote the Galatian Christians and pointed out what had happened to many of them since they first believed in Jesus “You are observing special days and months and seasons and years! I fear for you, that somehow I have wasted my efforts on you” (Galatians 4:10-11). In other words, they had allowed religious rules, that had nothing to do with their relationship with Jesus, to creep in and steal their joy. Paul put his finger on how their man-made religious system had affected them. He asked a pertinent question, “Where is that joyful and grateful spirit you felt then?” (Galatians
4:15, NLT). That’s a good question for any of us to ask if we lose our joy. What has happened to your joy?

Performance-Driven Religion is a Joy Killer
There is no greater example in the Bible of joyless religion than the religious leaders of Jesus’ day. They scrupulously observed the smallest details of religious rules but missed the Son of God who was standing in front of them teaching and healing. Jesus Himself described what they did to those who followed them. They weighed the people down with a heavy burden of man-made rules. Jesus pointed out the problem of the religious leaders when He addressed them. “Jesus replied, ‘And you experts in the law, woe to you, because you load people down with burdens they can hardly carry, and you yourselves will not lift one finger to help them’ ” (Luke 11:45). An example of this was provided by two rabbis who counted 1521 man-made laws their tradition had connected with the Sabbath. The religious leaders of Jesus’ day equated obeying these man-made traditions with obeying God’s Word.
 
Jesus Offers An Invitation of Grace
Jesus didn’t come to adjust their legalistic approach to religion. He came to replace that heavy burden with a life of freedom and joy. That is the message of God’s grace. Jesus had a message for those burdened by the religious loads placed on people by the religion of that day and it is a message for our day, too. “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). That is the gospel message. Come to Jesus! It’s that simple and yet profound. Faith in Jesus is what we need. We don’t need 1521 rules about the Sabbath; we simply need to believe in what He did for us that we couldn’t do for ourselves. We find many things we could say about our salvation in Scripture but they can all be summarized in this offer Jesus makes to all of us who’ve lost our joy in the struggle to do for ourselves what could have only been done by Jesus. Don’t get so lost in religious performance that you lose sight of Jesus and His gift of grace. He is who the gospel is all about and what He did for us on Calvary is enough to secure our eternal salvation. Believing in Him and what He did for us is what God wants from us. When we come to Jesus we discover what we always find when we experience God’s grace—inexpressible joy. Don’t let man-made religion steal your joy.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

8 important truths about surveillance

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

text:
Founders seeking venture capital:

Buyer beware.  

Can you imagine trying to build a huge company using dilutive financing, only to get into serious litigation with your own VC?

Hugely unproductive and energy sucking.

Let’s be honest, most of us (you 🫵) don’t need venture capital. You need revenue and to build a team. You need to grind.  That’s why I’m so bullish on HELOC founders. 

At the same time, this is a rich people problem.  “My $1BN series B was so over subscribed I didn’t want to include my early supporters”.  Like, that’s not a real problem. Same as being upset that your iPhone 18 is going to ship a week late.   Seriously, there are starving kids in the world and people got hit by a hurricane today. 

Based on Isaiah’s letter below, Valar absolutely violated their contract with the VC below.  They gave away rights in exchange for much needed capital.  That’s offer and consideration. I struggle to see how the court sides with Valar based on the argument: your honor, I didn’t want to honor the bargain I made, because I wanted to give Sequoia more.

There’s a lesson here. You have to be able to read your own contracts.  This takes experience and discipline.  I’m positive Isaiah read that clause multiple times, but never thought twice about it, until he regretted giving it to all his major shareholders, because he suddenly wanted something different.  Well, that’s not exactly how contracts work. When you contract you have to be able to picture the future. 

The voting of a majority of shareholders to strip the right is interesting.  There’s a chance that it’s lawful, but there’s a chance it’s not.  It’s either a genius move or it’s breach of contract.  To Isaiah’s point, the courts will decide.  The biggest problem was the timing, it was clearly done to circumvent and disadvantage the lone holdout, the day before the funding, in order to invalidate the prior agreement after the intention of Valar was clear.   My guess is there is case law on this is on the side of the VC and the timeline presented by the plaintiff will be brutal.

Preserve all records, texts, phone calls, and emails will be examined!

Again, if you don’t want to live by the inconvenient parts of the contract - don’t put it in the contract!

The biggest question, instead of instigating litigation, why not just honor the contract and give the VC the 5% pro rata they were due?  When did a handshake stop being a handshake?

There’s also serious risk that Isaiah’s letter below is tortious interference or defamation.   That can carry unwanted personal liability.  If Valar loses the first case, Isaiah very well could lose the second case.  Not worth the risk.

And yes, I know Isaiah was livid about the whole thing and his own lawyers gassed him up to sue in Delaware. He wanted to do what he thought was right, and the VC only cared about their profit.

I wish them both good luck and an equally sucky out of court settlement.  I hope not to read about it again.  It’s a clear case of buyer’s remorse.

There were more creative ways to solve this, like letting Sequoia buy out the VC and offering up warrants as additional compensation to the VC.

Prediction: Isaiah will have to pay them to go away and will later regret the whole thing. 

Benefit: Valar nuked (pun) their pro-rata spring back provision. 

Founder, you don’t need the headache of litigation, and you don’t need the headache of VC’s.

-your neighborhood engineer

text:
A specialty chemicals manufacturer expanding beyond textiles into oilfield chemicals, alongside home care, water treatment, construction and other industrial applications.

JM Small Cap Fund Regular Growth was the highest buyer of 300,000 shares in Aug 2026. 

Key Growth Trigger:

🛢️ CrudeChem Technologies (CCT) Acquisition

Fineotex acquired a 53.33% controlling stake in the US-based CrudeChem Technologies Group in December 2025, opening a new growth avenue in North American oilfield chemicals.

CCT brings manufacturing facilities, laboratories, customised formulations and technical support in Texas, strengthening Fineotex’s international presence and cross-selling opportunities.

Q1 FY27 Analysis:

Fineotex reported a sharp increase in revenue, reflecting the consolidation of CCT and growth in its existing business.

1. Strong revenue growth

Consolidated revenue reached ~₹387 Cr, up approximately 164% YoY.

2. Profitability improved, but more slowly

Net profit rose ~93% YoY to ₹48.2 Cr. Revenue grew much faster than profit, highlighting the need to monitor operating efficiency.

3. Oilfield chemicals emerging as a growth engine

The US acquisition diversifies Fineotex beyond its traditional textile chemicals business and provides access to new customers and markets.

4. Capacity expansion

Recent results analysis indicates total manufacturing capacity of approximately 1.48 lakh MTPA following expansion at the Texas facility.

Higher utilisation could support growth, provided customer demand and margins remain healthy.

Key factors to track:

⚡️Margins: 
EBITDA margin reportedly declined to ~15.7% in Q1 FY27. Can scale, pricing and operating leverage improve profitability?

⚡️Integration: 
Customer additions, capacity utilisation, cross-selling and efficient integration of CCT will be crucial.

⚡️Valuation: 
At ~₹6,500 Cr market cap, future growth must justify the valuation. Strong revenue growth alone is not enough.

The stock price has gained 200% from its 52 weeks low price. 

My personal View:

Fineotex is attempting a strategic transformation from a predominantly textile-focused chemicals business into a more diversified specialty chemicals player.

The CCT acquisition offers meaningful growth potential, but execution, margin recovery and valuation will determine whether that potential translates into sustainable shareholder value.

The next few quarters will be important to watch.

text:
Mount for Purse or Escarcelle

这件名为“钱包或挂袋边框”的金属工艺品，创作于约1559年，出自西班牙艺术家Diego de Çaias的作坊。尺寸为19 x 13.9厘米，整体采用钢质打造，并饰以精细的金嵌工艺。该作品本质上是一个钱包或挂袋的边框，用以固定附着于皮革或织物制成的钱袋，典型地由男性佩戴于腰间，其悬挂设计通过转轴联系，实现携带的便利性。

作品装饰以丰富的狩猎及军事场景图案，表现了当时西班牙贵族社会对这些主题的关注和喜好。最引人注意的是刻有“ALFONSVS ESTENSIS”的铭文，结合盾形纹章，明确指明了其所属者为阿方索二世·埃斯特家族成员，他即于1559年荣膺费拉拉公爵。这一铭文不仅为艺术品提供了确凿的身份标识，也为研究这件作品的历史背景提供了重要线索。

从工艺角度看，钢材的锻造配合细致的金镶嵌技术，展示出了十六世纪中期欧洲金属工艺的高超水平。观看者应特别留意转轴结构及其铭文位置，这是设计上的功能性特点，同时作为装饰焦点，具有双重意义。边框的整体形态平衡，纹章与图案布局均匀，显示出制作师对细节的严谨把握。

这件装饰边框既反映了文艺复兴时期贵族配饰的风格与实用需求，也体现了身份认同与地位象征的文化内涵。在观赏这一作品时，除了其精湛工艺，铭文与纹章更是理解其历史价值的关键。展品现藏于中世纪艺术部门，是由Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance捐赠，曾归法国收藏家Frank Gair Macomber所有。整体而言，这件收藏品提供了丰富的视觉与文献资料，对于研究西班牙及意大利文艺复兴时期的贵族生活与工艺艺术具有重要意义。

This object, titled "Mount for Purse or Escarcelle," dates from around 1559 and originates from the workshop of Diego de Çaias, a Spanish artist whose activity likely centered in Antwerp. It measures 19 by 13.9 centimeters and is constructed from steel with gold inlay, exemplifying the high-quality metalworking techniques of mid-16th century Europe.

Functionally, the mount served as a frame for a small purse or escarcelle made of leather or cloth. These purses were typically worn by men at the waist, suspended by a swivel loop that allowed for ease of movement. The engineering behind the swivel suspension is both practical and decorative, providing a point of interest where the inscription is placed.

The decorative theme features carefully rendered scenes of hunting and military activities, motifs popular among the aristocracy during the Renaissance period. Most notably, the inscription "ALFONSVS ESTENSIS" appears on the swivel suspension loop, directly linking the object to Alfonso II d'Este, who was made Duke of Ferrara in 1559. The presence of his coat-of-arms further authenticates the connection to this prominent noble family. This identification offers valuable context about the wallet’s owner and adds historical significance to the piece.

From a craftsmanship perspective, the juxtaposition of robust steel with intricate gold inlay highlights the technical skill involved. Observers should pay particular attention to the swivel suspension mechanism, not only for its mechanical function but also because it acts as a focal point conveying the noble identity through inscription and heraldry. The overall balance of form and decorative elements demonstrates meticulous attention to detail by the artist’s workshop.

This purse mount encapsulates the blend of utility and status symbolism typical of Renaissance aristocratic accessories. Beyond its artistic merits, the inscription and heraldic emblem serve as key evidence for understanding the cultural and social milieu of the period. The object is housed within the Department of Medieval Art, gifted by Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance after previously being owned by collector Frank Gair Macomber. In sum, this mount offers rich insights into the material culture and artistic sophistication of Spanish and Italian Renaissance nobility.

text:
Grok Build just got a monster update......this one pushes long-running agents, browser workflows, worktrees, hooks, permissions, and session recovery much further

Background workflows can now be listed, stopped and resumed directly with /workflow, headless Grok waits for background goals and reports their outcome, Chrome profiles can persist across restarts, browser tabs can restore on demand, and workspace sessions can share browser cookies + storage

There’s also a new /density control for tool-call detail, persistent domain approvals for web fetches, live slash-command updates when skills change, and secure request forms that can collect sensitive details like passwords or card numbers without sending those values to the model

Underneath that is a massive hardening pass: cancel/edit-resend no longer unexpectedly reverts workspace files, long prompts are offloaded safely, worktrees recover and clean up more reliably, hooks and approval flows are tighter, browser state is more stable, background agents respect saved approvals, and resume/worktree performance is much faster

Release Notes: v1.0.51

Breaking Changes

• Cancel and edit-resend on long sessions no longer unexpectedly revert workspace files.
• Memory settings simplified: rollout and file_writes_enabled options removed; memory is on or off.
• Removed the /share command and related session sharing features from the CLI and SDK.

Features

• Inline viewports can now be restored at a previously saved screen area without extra cursor queries.
• Headless grok -p now waits for background goals to finish and reports their outcome.
• /imagine and similar commands now run the matching bundled skill when the required tools are unavailable.
• New /density command and Tool call density setting let you choose how much detail tool calls show in the transcript.
• Web fetch approval cards now include "always allow" and "never allow" domain options that persist for the folder.
• Slash command completion now updates live when skills are added or changed during a session.
• Request form now securely collects and fills sensitive details like passwords or card numbers without sending values to the model.
• Chrome profiles can now be persisted across restarts using durable state directories.
• Workspace server sessions now share one Chrome instance for cookies and storage.
• /feedback Drafts tab now supports G / Home and End to jump to the first or last draft.
• Pinned sessions on the dashboard now stay in the order you pinned or reordered them.
• Shift+Enter, Ctrl+., Ctrl+/ and Ctrl+[ / ] now work inside tmux when extended-keys are enabled.
• grok -p --output-format json now reports the exact worktree folder used (useful after -w name collisions).
• Bare hook commands such as my-guard now run from PATH when not found next to the hook file.
• Headless JSON error output now includes the worktree folder when a session was started.
• grok sessions list and /resume now show worktree sessions started from the same subfolder.
• /exit (and aliases) in a dashboard details view now closes only that session instead of quitting Grok.
• Editors offering file access now receive a one-time transcript notice that the agent reads and writes disk files.
• --background-wait-timeout now also stops an active headless goal after the timeout and exits with an error.
• Interactive sessions now include the Grok Build user guide location so the agent can answer usage questions.
• New /workflow commands let you list, stop, and resume background workflow runs without sending them to the model.
• Background workflow runs now appear in the tasks pane with a stop button.
• Hooks that ask about web searches or file deletes now show the hook name on the approval card.
• config.toml now accepts an [update] section without breaking other commands.
• Hook load errors listed in /hooks can now be expanded to see the full message.
• grok worktree commands now work correctly inside Jujutsu repositories.
• Images pasted with skill commands like /pr-workflow are now sent to the model.
• Pressing Ctrl+C on a goal now pauses the goal instead of letting it continue.
• grok -p now runs auth_provider_command when no login is stored.
• Reopening a chat with an active goal now continues the goal automatically.
• Browser tabs can now be restored on demand instead of all at once when a session resumes.
• grok agent stdio now supports listing sessions via ACP and returns consistent reply envelopes.
• Answering an approval with a message now tells the model it is a follow-up.
• --allowed-tools is now accepted as an alias for --allow in headless mode.

Bug Fixes

• Slash command suggestions no longer make the text after the cursor disappear while typing.
• Running workflows in the dock now show the same pulsing indicator as in the main scrollback.
• Mode switch tool calls now appear in the transcript with the target mode name.
• Always-approve mode now automatically approves web requests without extra prompts.
• The follow indicator no longer appears when only blank padding sits below the viewport.
• Search failures now keep the original pattern instead of showing an empty Search "".
• Sessions that open without a model list now use the public Auto id and succeed on every account.
• Background wake turns that request plan changes or mode switches are now handled correctly.
• Model-call retries now show progress status instead of a generic waiting message.
• Foreground subagent activity now appears correctly after resume.
• Very large pasted prompts are now offloaded to a file instead of being sent inline.
• Sign-in failures now show a clear plain-English message with the next step instead of raw errors.
• Logging out now stops any running turns on local sessions instead of leaving them active.
• The send-now shortcut no longer accidentally enables always-approve mode while a permission card is open.
• /find now keeps match counts and navigation accurate while replies or command output stream in.
• Images from tools are now validated so bad files no longer break the current turn or future replays.
• Screenshots and other image artifacts saved by the browser tool are now stored as real image files.
• Rate-limit errors now show the expected message; very small images are rejected early.
• Send-now (Ctrl+Enter) no longer accidentally answers an open question card.
• Opening the queue with Up now scrolls so the selected follow-up is visible.
• Command output that contains clear-screen codes is no longer discarded.
• Dashboard cursor and overlay counter now correctly track the active grouping view.
• Headless JSON output now reports the correct stop reason when the turn limit is reached and removes duplicate error prefixes.
• Session picker footer no longer lists the same shortcut twice.
• Dragging images from a file manager onto terminals like GNOME Terminal or xfce4-terminal now attaches them correctly.
• Plan comments added while a revision runs are now preserved and sent when the plan is approved.
• Permission prompts that fail now show a clearer message without blaming the interface.
• --disallowed-tools now accepts the exact names shown to the model (run_terminal_command, spawn_subagent, etc.).
• Long pastes without bracketed-paste markers are now read completely instead of stalling after ~1 KB.
• A feedback send now shows "Sending feedback…" immediately; failed sends no longer repeat the lead phrase.
• Typing, arrows or Enter while an approval card appears no longer accidentally approve the action or enable always-approve mode.
• Error hints for legacy session import now appear in full instead of being cut off by the pager.
• Skills in the folder where grok started now correctly show as (local).
• Worktree creation no longer hangs when the repo contains named pipes or sockets.
• --no-subagents flag now works correctly in headless / -p sessions.
• Resumed sessions now correctly show aborted subagent tasks as cancelled instead of failed.
• Large parallel shell batches no longer drop calls with "hook state lost" errors.
• Write approval cards now show the existing file contents that will be replaced.
• Slash command completion now shows the correct name for files under commands/ instead of always showing /commands.
• PreToolUse hooks now validate rewrites against the tool schema and deny invalid ones before running the tool.
• Ctrl+C during a turn now cancels the turn even when a modal such as /mcps or the block viewer is open.
• grok -w now opens the session at the worktree root (with a note) when the original launch folder does not exist in the new worktree.
• /cd and the location picker now accept quoted or escaped folder paths.
• Web search hooks now fire under the correct web_search name and carry query.
• Large file writes or many screenshots no longer end the session.
• Glob tool hooks now match under list_dir and carry the correct directory.
• /find now scrolls to the exact wrapped row containing the current match.
• Downloads via FetchMcpResource are now refused in plan mode and resolve paths consistently.
• Pinned dashboard sessions now survive restarts and layout changes instead of disappearing from the saved list.
• Slash commands like /imagine now work regardless of capitalization and correctly substitute skills when tools are missing.
• Turning off bypass mode without naming a session now correctly restores prompts in all open sessions.
• /delete with extra text now shows an error instead of deleting the current session.
• Failed /feedback status messages now wrap inside the dialog instead of clipping at the border.
• Number-key picks in the dashboard peek no longer leak to the wrong agent after Up/Down navigation.
• Worktrees created with -w are now correctly tracked and resumable even when GROK_HOME is reached through a symlink.
• grok worktree rm and gc now clean up names after manually deleting a worktree folder so -w NAME works again.
• Hook scripts that read stdin with read now receive a complete line.
• A policy that disables non-managed hooks now applies to the next session instead of only after restart.
• /resume and grok sessions list no longer show worktree sessions from a sibling submodule or separate-git-dir repo.
• A hook listed under two different matchers now runs only once per tool call.
• Typing a hidden command such as /cd in a session and pressing Enter now runs it instead of accepting a near-match skill.
• @-file completion no longer accepts a match from an earlier query when you type quickly.
• Tool hooks now run one at a time per session and stop promptly on cancel or exit.
• PostToolUse hooks now receive a correct whole-millisecond duration.
• PreToolUse hooks for shell commands now see the model's block_until_ms value.
• MCP tool calls now show hook permission prompts and cards name the hook that asked.
• Typing while a permission or ask card is visible no longer selects or answers the card.
• grok worktree list now shows unfinished copies left by an interrupted create.
• Auto mode now asks before deleting files that the classifier has not already allowed.
• Fixed intermittent List/Read/Open failures during concurrent v2 hardening migrations.
• grok -p -s with a reused session id now shows the plain refusal message instead of JSON-RPC noise.
• Settings saves no longer re-insert the built-in default fork model into config.toml.
• Fixed several pager rows that showed wrong paths, truncated names, or hid failure/cancel states.
• --system-prompt now correctly appends rules from --append-system-prompt instead of dropping them.
• /new now inherits always-approve mode from the tab it was run from instead of another tab.
• Multi-select questions now let you toggle several answers with number keys before submitting.
• Slash-command notices typed while a reply streams no longer hide the streaming reply.
• @ file search no longer accepts keys or moves the highlight while results are still updating.
• Worktree db rebuild now restores names so rm and show by name work again.
• A prompt blocked by a hook no longer titles the session.
• Background subagents now respect saved approvals and --always-approve after the parent turn finishes.
• Per-session system prompt overrides now correctly use only the session's own rules.
• Connection stalled errors now show a clearer message with network advice.
• Invalid model provider tables now produce a clear startup error instead of silent fallback.
• Narrow feedback dialog now shows full draft titles and readable confirm prompts.
• /workflow stop|resume <name> now correctly targets the live run instead of an ended first run.
• Dialogs like /feedback no longer disappear on very short terminal windows.
• Delete operations now respect the same permission rules as shell rm commands.
• Hooks can no longer rewrite a web-search call to restrict domains.
• Workspace server now starts with per-session private Chrome by default.
• Notification hooks for permission prompts and task completion now run reliably before a headless session exits.
• Headless goal runs no longer print a spurious "Goal paused" message after completion.
• Legacy UI density settings now combine correctly across config tiers and produce expected folding.
• Approval answers sent after a turn ends no longer affect the turn.
• Background shell commands now fail immediately when the working directory does not exist.
• grok worktree rm without -f now safely keeps worktrees when the unsaved-work check fails or times out.
• The dashboard slash menu now shows skills from the home session even when opened early.
• grok worktree rm and gc now correctly remove worktrees whose only untracked content is empty folders.
• Editing a queued prompt now prevents accidental removal with a stale client view.
• The model is now told when memory is turned off or on for the session.
• Hook results in the UI now correctly distinguish between notes and tool outcomes.
• Permission cards for MCP tools can no longer be tricked into showing fake option rows.
• The agent stdio mode now returns clearer errors for malformed client requests and consistent recap replies.
• Scroll logging and acceleration calculations no longer produce backwards timestamps under load.
• Hooks and tool commands started from the TUI can no longer read or write the interactive terminal.
• Delete operations now correctly match Bash(rm …) ask/deny rules even when the path contains .. or the cwd is a symlink.
• Web search and image approval cards now only offer always-approve mode to clients that support it.
• Closing a session in the dashboard no longer leaves it listed under Inactive.
• Running /compact on an empty session no longer resets the reported context window.
• With goals disabled, a headless /goal line is now treated as a normal prompt instead of failing.
• Background shell commands no longer flip back to running when late output arrives.
• Only slash commands at the start of a message trigger skills.
• Browser tabs restore and close more reliably with fewer races.
• Fast model names in the footer no longer show double parentheses.
• SubagentStart and Notification hook activity is no longer reported to the UI.
• Voice error messages now display with correct punctuation.
• disable_zdr_incompatible_tools changes now apply to new turns without restarting the worker.
• Project skills are now labeled correctly for nested projects.

Performance

• Opening the resume picker is now much faster on machines with many worktrees.
• grok worktree commands start faster by skipping unnecessary model catalog work at boot.

text:
Grok Build just got one of its biggest updates yet.....a massive upgrade touching almost every part of the agent stack

Compact mode gets a major upgrade, timestamps are now configurable, shell commands clearly show when they’re running or finished, tables can export directly as TSV, CSV or Markdown, and the dashboard now gives much better visibility and control over worktrees

Under the hood, the update is even bigger: stalled model calls now retry, long sessions are more resilient, permission handling is much tighter, failed file writes preserve existing contents, CJK memory search improves, concurrent config edits are safer, MCP tool discovery is more reliable, and worktree creation + deletion gets a huge reliability pass

There’s even a breaking safety change: grok worktree rm now refuses to delete active worktrees or ones with unsaved changes unless you explicitly force it

Release Notes: v1.0.50

Breaking Changes:
• grok worktree rm without -f now refuses to delete worktrees that are in use or contain unsaved changes and exits with an error.

Features:
• Compact mode now collapses recaps and keeps inner spacing on tall terminals.
• Clicking the git branch in the header now copies the full branch name.
• Long branch names now abbreviate on narrow terminals while remaining copyable.
• Targeted cancels now stop only the specific response when requested by clients.
• Compact mode now hides the dock (or tasks pane) the same way Ctrl+G does.
• New timestamps setting offers off, minimal, and on modes in Settings and /timestamps.
• Shell command output now shows "Running …" while executing and "Ran …" when finished.
• Live preview pins now include whether an app was observed behind the URL.
• Command palette (Ctrl+P) and model picker now open at the same width as the settings modal.
• Tables rendered by grok now show copy buttons underneath that export clean TSV, CSV or Markdown suitable for spreadsheets.
• Dashboard now shows which worktree each session belongs to, displays the -m model in the new-agent box, and lets you toggle worktree mode in the folder picker.

Bug Fixes:
• Shell permission decisions now correctly prompt or approve commands matching the permission manager.
• Cancelled turns now correctly mark unanswered tool calls as cancelled instead of succeeded.
• Long error messages in the /usage and /session-info modals now wrap instead of being truncated.
• Em-dashes no longer appear in status messages and subagent rows.
• Stalled model calls during turns now retry before failing the turn.
• Queue pane and Ctrl+; now appear and work when the dock is hidden with Ctrl+G.
• Long sessions no longer disconnect when the conversation exceeds 4 MiB.
• Permission rules now accept native tool names such as run_terminal_command and Shell.
• /rewind now places the cursor at the end of the restored prompt.
• Failed file writes now leave the previous contents instead of an empty file.
• Fixed /loop and scheduler_create so non-ASCII intervals like 5分 no longer crash the session.
• Fixed --disallowed-tools when only one scheduler tool is named; the other two no longer cause startup failure.
• Fixed closing a busy tab so queued prompts are no longer sent to the model.
• Fixed relative --cwd so grok --cwd a no longer ends up running inside a/a.
• The terminal title now shows "Action Required" for any background session waiting on approval.
• grok now accepts a prompt via piped stdin in headless mode instead of trying to open the UI.
• An admin-set [features] title_refresh = false in requirements.toml now correctly disables title refresh even when GROK_TITLE_REFRESH is set.
• Custom notification commands defined under [[ui.notifications.hooks]] now execute on matching events.
• An admin pin of [cli] use_leader = false now correctly prevents --leader from starting a leader process.
• When multiple MCP servers expose a tool with the same name, search_tool now returns all of them.
• Concurrent Grok windows editing settings no longer lose or corrupt config.toml entries such as MCP servers or permission rules.
• web_fetch no longer downloads huge files into memory before rejecting them.
• memory_get no longer returns huge files that exceed the read limit.
• Continue to run no longer kills commands running inside background subagents.
• memory_search now finds Japanese, Chinese, and Korean words inside longer notes.
• Drafts saved by the model now appear under their actual titles in /feedback.
• Imagine replies that are not valid images are now rejected instead of being saved as .jpg files.
• A workflow file that fails to parse now reports the exact file and parse error instead of 'unknown workflow'.
• Re-encoded images are now oriented correctly using their EXIF tags instead of appearing sideways.
• Image and log paths reported after /fork --worktree now point to real files instead of missing locations.
• Tab characters in terminal command output are now preserved when shown to the model.
• Transparent images are now kept as PNG when re-encoded instead of turning black.
• The bundled ripgrep is now available to terminal commands even on images that do not install it.
• Request bodies now stay under a small configured max_request_bytes limit instead of growing past it.
• Effort level now stays the same after a bare /model switch instead of jumping to the new model's default.
• Ctrl+\ and other modified digits no longer accidentally select options on permission or cancel cards.
• Feedback submissions now show accurate success or failure messages without premature thanks or duplicated prefixes.
• grok doctor now reports the exact config file or setting that prevents Grok from starting instead of saying zero issues.
• Recap summaries now appear on screen automatically instead of requiring manual scrolling.
• grok doctor fix now opens its confirmation card on Cancel to prevent accidental edits to shell or tmux config.
• Slash commands now run regardless of case (e.g. /COMPACT or /Compact).
• /context no longer shows an invented auto-compact threshold when the agent does not report one.
• Agent text no longer keeps the pager redrawing when a tool call interrupts the sentence.
• CLI tool calls no longer fail or overflow when the workspace directory is deleted or output is huge.
• Logs written to files or when NO_COLOR is set are now plain text instead of containing color codes.
• Prompts now fail immediately with a clear message if the session's working directory no longer exists instead of failing later or recreating it.
• grok -w now works correctly with separate-git-dir repositories and shows clear errors when run outside a git repo or on an empty repo.
• Shell tool descriptions now correctly state the actual output truncation limit, and grep respects globs relative to the current session directory.
• Compaction messages now scroll into view instead of appearing below the bottom of the screen after a turn finishes.
• Git-mode worktrees created with -w now preserve uncommitted changes instead of dropping them.
• Worktrees created with --worktree-ref no longer contain wrong submodule contents or LFS pointer text.
• Worktree creation now shows the same clear error messages on every code path.
• Failed worktree creates now show a clear error on the home screen instead of being hidden.
• Merge and rebase conflicts now appear in the changes list instead of being hidden.
• Fixed a crash when starting a new session with durable rewind checkpoints enabled.
• Managed permission files with one bad key no longer lose all their valid rules.
• Simultaneous worktree creates with the same label now succeed instead of one failing with "already exists".
• grok worktree rm without -f no longer deletes arbitrary folders that happen to share a name with a removed worktree.
• Discard now affects only the exact files you select instead of also deleting or reverting similarly-named files.
• Permission rules with one bad entry no longer lose the other rules in the same section.
• Chat Completions streams that end without a finish reason are now retried instead of returning partial output.
• grok worktree rm by label now refuses when the label exists in multiple repos.
• Grep now respects Read deny rules that use a leading ./.

Performance:
• Command hooks no longer cause large memory spikes when they print a lot of output.
• Retry waits now vary between processes instead of being identical.
